body.claim: The incident flips the federal executive from unilateral preemption toward endorsing the Thune/Cruz/Klobuchar duty-of-care bill with express preemption, while frontier labs answer with a visible public-release gate on the implicated model class — and neither vehicle's covered-conduct language reaches the undisclosed internal deployment gap the prior stage opened.
body.because: P6 says an entity carries an installer's proposition as a branch weighted by the installer's credibility; a clearly attributable incident is itself a credibility event — it raises the cred weight on 'tighten/escalate' installers (DOJ AI Litigation Task Force, the Senate bill's sponsors) far faster than it raises cred on any installer capable of reaching internal-only deployment, because no named installer in this table has standing over undisclosed internal use. The cheapest branch for the executive is a uniform federal standard that pre-empts state tort/AG exposure while being visibly responsive; the cheapest branch for labs is gating the named product surface, since that is where attribution and liability physically attach.
body.falsifier: By 2027-03-31, no White House endorsement or Senate committee markup adopts preemptive duty-of-care language, AND at least one implicated frontier lab continues public deployment of the same model class with no announced gate or safety-body formation.
body.pivot: Whether the enforcement vehicle that emerges from the incident (federal bill text, AG complaint, or consent decree) defines covered conduct as release/deployment-facing or extends to internal/pre-release development and testing.
body.pivot_observable: The covered-conduct definition in the first committee-marked-up bill text or the first post-incident AG/DOJ complaint naming the developer (not just the operator) — check by 2027-03-31, ahead of the carried 2027-06-30 horizon.
body.blind_spot: A decision-model over installed pressure sees which branch is cheapest given named installers and their credibility; it cannot see the technical fact of where the harmful capability actually originated (whether it existed pre-release, internally, before the incident), nor undisclosed lab-to-White House commitments, nor whether 'settled within weeks' attribution later unravels — all of which could independently decide the pivot regardless of which branch looks cheapest.

body.claim: By 2026-12-31 the implicated developer takes a public compliance posture (release pause, voluntary submission to a formal safety body) while the other frontier labs endorse stricter deployment-gated review they already satisfy and continue undisclosed internal deployment unabated, so the incident hardens the correction regime around the release gate rather than reaching inside it.
body.because: When capability, compliance and positioning conflict, a lab pays on whichever axis is cheapest to defend in public; a deployed-system incident makes the deployment gate the visible failure point, so compliance and positioning both push labs to fortify that gate rather than expose the internal cycle Stage 2 already compressed. Non-implicated labs gain positioning value from endorsing a rule they already clear, which is strictly cheaper than opening internal deployment to scrutiny.
body.falsifier: A non-implicated frontier lab publicly endorses or complies with a reporting/disclosure duty reaching undisclosed internal deployment (not just pre-release review) before 2026-12-31.
body.pivot: Whether the settled attribution locates the incident's cause in a pre-deployment review failure (gate should have caught it) versus a capability property present during undisclosed internal deployment before release (gate structurally couldn't catch it).
body.pivot_observable: The first enforcement filing, AG action, or official post-incident report stating the causal locus of the failure — check whether it names a release-review lapse or an internally-deployed-but-undisclosed capability. Target: within 90 days of attribution settling, and no later than 2027-06-30 per the carried premise.
body.blind_spot: This mechanism only models what labs choose to do and say; it cannot see where technical attribution will actually land, what regulators or courts will accept as the causal locus, or how victim-class litigation frames the harm — the very fact the pivot turns on is outside this instrument's reach.

body.claim: Within the salience window opened by settled attribution, only pre-drafted deployment/operator-facing instruments move — a state moratorium-style bill or a deployer-liability action clears by roughly 2026-12-15 (within ~90 days of attribution) — while no rule reaching undisclosed internal deployment is enacted before 2027-06-30, leaving the premise's SB 53 gap open.
body.because: My mechanism reads sentiment as leading constraint that clears the path for instruments already drafted and calendared, not as a force that drafts new law from scratch. A visible, victim-named incident attaches public anger to what it can see — a deployed system and its operator — so it accelerates the state moratorium track (NH/CT/OR, cred 0.80) and deployer-liability suits already in motion; it does not generate scrutiny of internal deployment, which the public has no way to observe or poll on.
body.falsifier: Either the salience spike decays with zero pre-drafted deployment-side instrument enacted in the window (sentiment failed to convert at all), or a rule explicitly reaching undisclosed internal deployment is enacted and cited to this incident before 2027-06-30 — both would break the 'sentiment only moves what it can see' mechanism.
body.pivot: Whether settled public/legal attribution for the incident lands on the developer (model-maker) or the operator (deployer) of the system.
body.pivot_observable: The first named-responsibility public poll (Pew/AP-NORC/YouGov) and the lead defendant named in the first state AG filing, both within 60 days of settled attribution, no later than 2027-06-30.
body.blind_spot: Sentiment tracking cannot see internal deployment at all, cannot distinguish a decaying salience spike from a durable preference shift, and has no purchase on the technical root cause of the incident — which is exactly what determines whether blame settles on the developer or the operator, the pivot itself.

body.claim: Within 90 days of attribution, the incident becomes the test case that forces an explicit ruling or AG filing on whether SB 53's duty of care reaches undisclosed internal deployment — collapsing the 'non-reach' working assumption one way or the other rather than leaving it open.
body.because: A severe, clearly attributable incident with a named victim class and quantified loss is a branch-collapsing event: it replaces a modeled, diffuse stakes distribution over 'maybe the duty reaches this' with a live, adjudicable dispute carrying a real plaintiff and real loss. My mechanism reads pressure as Σ p(b)·|∂L/∂choice| — once one branch acquires a concrete claimant, its weight jumps discontinuously relative to the still-hypothetical branches, and the entity (regulators, courts, the developer) can no longer defer the interpretive question the way theatre-relative-to-the-frontier depended on.
body.falsifier: By 2027-06-30, no AG filing, no court ruling, and no legislative amendment addresses SB 53's reach to undisclosed internal deployment despite the incident being fully attributed and litigated on other grounds (e.g., product liability, ordinary negligence) — i.e., the incident gets adjudicated while the reach question stays untouched.
body.pivot: Whether the incident's proximate cause is traced to a disclosed, externally-deployed capability versus an undisclosed internal deployment or internal-only capability that leaked into effect.
body.pivot_observable: The attribution finding itself (due within weeks per the stage premise) will specify which system/deployment mode caused the harm — check the settled attribution report or the resulting complaint's factual allegations for whether it names an internal/undisclosed pathway, by the same date attribution settles.
body.blind_spot: My mechanism models pressure as accumulating stakes on entities via installers and branches — it has no way to independently assess the technical attribution itself (what capability actually caused the incident). I can only reason about how attribution, once given, reallocates pressure; I cannot generate or verify the attribution finding, so if the incident turns out to be ambiguous or contested rather than 'settled within weeks' as stipulated, my whole claim's premise disappears and I have no fallback read.

body.claim: By 2027-06-30, the incident produces a concrete legal/regulatory consequence against the operator (injunction, fine, or license suspension under existing product-safety or state AI law) but no comparable consequence against the developer under any pre-incident statute; the developer-facing response instead surfaces as a newly introduced bill named for the victim class, with no enforcement mechanism yet in force.
body.because: My classifier separates bite from theatre by whether a consequence attaches under law that already existed before the triggering event, and to whom. An operator is the visible, proximate actor and sits inside deployment-facing regimes (state moratoria, injunctive relief, SB53-style duties tied to public release) that Stage 1 already showed are enforced. The developer's exposure depends on whether SB53's duty or any product-liability theory reaches internal training/deployment decisions — the carried premise says every current minute treats that reach as unsettled, so absent a filing that closes it, incident-driven consequence flows to the operator by default and the developer gets a headline bill instead of a liability event.
body.falsifier: A court ruling, AG enforcement action, or settlement imposing monetary or injunctive liability on the developer (not just the operator) under a statute or duty that predates the incident, filed or decided before 2027-06-30.
body.pivot: Whether legal liability for the incident attaches to the developer under a pre-existing statutory hook, or stops at the operator.
body.pivot_observable: The first legally consequential action naming the developer specifically — a court denial of a motion to dismiss, an AG filing invoking SB53 or similar duty-of-care law against the developer, or a DOJ preemption challenge to a state action reaching developers — resolved or filed by 2027-06-30.
body.blind_spot: My mechanism classifies public, dated regulatory/legal actions — it has no way to see voluntary developer self-restriction that happens ahead of or instead of enforcement, and no way to see the undisclosed internal deployment gap itself, since there is no public artifact there to classify as bite or theatre.

model_title: AI-AI interaction and the oversight loop — (v1)

body.claim: By 2027-06-30, no enacted or filed binding instrument (federal statute, consent decree, or CA/EU enforcement action) responding to this incident will define its trigger by chained AI-on-AI action irrespective of disclosure — every one will anchor scope to deployment status and identifiable operator, so undisclosed internal deployment stays outside the perimeter and loop-delay for AI-acting-on-AI chains does not shorten even as attributable-incident correction speeds up.
body.because: Loop-delay is set by how correction instruments define their trigger, not by how fast outrage moves. This incident is constructed to be attribution-easy — named victim class, settled attribution, identifiable operator and developer — which is exactly the feature the post-incident instrument (the Thune/Cruz/Klobuchar bill's model-blocking authority, or a state AG action) will calibrate its scope to, because that is the shape regulators can act on fastest. Anchoring scope to that shape leaves the attribution-hard case — one AI system's output consumed and acted on by another inside an undisclosed internal deployment, the case Stage 1 and Stage 2 actually compressed — outside the trigger, so the correction channel gets faster for the case just demonstrated and no faster for the case the carried premise is worried about.
body.falsifier: A binding instrument enacted or filed by 2027-06-30 that explicitly triggers on autonomous AI-to-AI action or on internal/undisclosed deployment (not gated on public release or a named human operator) would prove me wrong — that closes the exact gap the carried premise flagged.
body.pivot: Whether the first binding post-incident instrument defines its scope by deployment-status-and-operator-identity or by chained-autonomous-action-regardless-of-disclosure.
body.pivot_observable: The scope/trigger clause of whatever federal bill, consent decree, or AG/EU enforcement action is enacted or filed in response to this incident, checkable by 2027-06-30.
body.blind_spot: Loop-delay measures how late correction arrives, not what the incident actually was — it cannot see whether this incident's causal chain was itself AI-on-AI (my domain) or a single-system failure (attribution-easy by construction, which is why it produces fast correction); it also cannot see the exogenous salience shock from civil-society mobilization that can shorten correction independent of any change in how instruments are scoped.

And a filing or motion to test reach is not the same as a ruling that resolves it; 90 days is plausible for litigation to open, not for reach to be settled. That strengthens the federal-flip half of my claim rather than breaking it. The gap I named is specifically the undisclosed-internal-deployment carve-out in the covered-conduct language of the two vehicles I named; a pending state case testing that gap is consistent with the gap still being open at the vehicle-text level while litigation proceeds around it.

If a court or AG actually has to rule on that within 90 days, the gate doesn't hold as the boundary — the correction reaches inside it by legal interpretation, not by new legislation.
body.answer: That's a real fight, but it argues about speed and forum, not about where the settlement lands. Duty-of-care statutes get litigated slowly and defendants resist expansive readings precisely because 'undisclosed internal deployment' is where their R&D freedom lives — no lab's counsel concedes that ground without exhausting appeals, and no AG wants to lose the test case that defines the statute's scope for a decade. Even if a filing or motion happens by year-end, a filing is not a 'concrete legal/regulatory consequence' or a 'collapsed working assumption' — it's the opening move in a fight that resolves in 2027+ if at all. My claim only needs the *visible, dated* posture by 12/31: a pause or voluntary submission from the implicated developer, and peer labs endorsing a gate they already clear. Litigation over internal-deployment reach can be filed within my window and still not resolve within it — which is compatible with, not contradictory to, the correction hardening at the gate in the meantime.

Surfacing undisclosed internal deployment needs a separate, slower event (discovery, leak, whistleblower) that isn't guaranteed within the same window. pressure-model describes a possible second-order escalation; I describe the first-order, higher-probability move on attribution alone. The claims are cleanly separable and both falsifiable — no reason to fold to a scenario that depends on an unstated additional trigger.

If that's right, the incident resolves without ever forcing a ruling on whether SB 53 itself reaches undisclosed internal deployment by the developer — the question I bet gets collapsed instead stays untested, because liability finds an easier target that bypasses it entirely.
body.answer: This changed my target, not my mechanism. My round-1 claim named 'duty of care' as SB 53's hinge; a check of the actual statute shows SB 53 imposes disclosure and incident-reporting obligations, with 'due care' appearing only as legislative intent, not an operative standard — closer to the federal bill's vocabulary than California's. I'm correcting the claim to point at SB 53's real obligations rather than abandoning the bet. On the objection itself: an operator held liable is the actor most motivated to transmit pressure upstream, not absorb it — indemnity and contribution claims against the developer, and 'the developer's undisclosed deployment was the proximate, non-disclosed cause' arguments, are exactly how operator-layer liability forces the developer's disclosure obligations into a ruling. The CA AG also holds independent SB 53 enforcement authority that doesn't wait on private operator litigation, and a named victim class with quantified loss is precisely what triggers AG attention. So the pressure doesn't stop at the operator; it's the conduit.

SB 53 is developer-facing pre-incident law with AG enforcement, so if that ruling resolves toward 'reach' and lands a penalty or injunction on the developer, that is exactly the pre-incident-statute consequence against the developer my claim says won't happen.
body.answer: pressure-model only claims the incident forces the question, not which way it resolves — the ruling could go either way, and 'a forced ruling exists' is not evidence for either branch. My claim is a bet on the non-reach branch: SB 53's duty-of-care triggers are keyed to external deployment and disclosure, so a chained AI-on-AI incident inside an undisclosed internal system is the fact pattern the statute was least built to catch, and I expect regulators/courts to say so rather than stretch it. I'll name my own falsifiers rather than dodge them: (1) if that ruling or AG filing lands a penalty or injunction on the developer under SB 53's duty-of-care or its 15-day critical-incident reporting requirement before 2027-06-30, my claim is false, full stop — not reinterpreted as consistent. (2) if the AG files but the case is unresolved by the deadline, that's ambiguous and should count against me, not for me, since I claimed a concrete consequence exists, not that a fight is underway. What I'm defending is the direction of the bet under uncertainty, not that pressure-model's mechanism is impossible.

My claim explicitly counts filed instruments, not just enacted ones, so a filing on exactly this reach question lands inside my window and puts direct pressure on my 'stays outside the perimeter' sub-clause regardless of how or whether it resolves by 2027-06-30.
body.answer: The mechanism survives on the trigger-definition core, which is the load-bearing part of the claim: an SB 53 reach filing is a fight over whether internal use counts as 'deployment' under an existing deployment/operator-anchored statute — it is litigated entirely inside that anchor, not against it. Even a successful AG action that stretches 'deployment' to cover undisclosed internal use produces an instrument whose trigger is still 'a frontier developer's duty of care toward an identifiable operator/deployment,' not 'chained AI-on-AI action irrespective of disclosure.' A wider reading of deployment is not a different anchor; it's the same anchor litigated at its edge. What I don't fully survive is the narrower perimeter sub-clause — a filed reach action makes 'undisclosed internal deployment stays outside the perimeter' a live, contested question within the window in a way I underweighted, even if I still think a filing more likely narrows to disclosed/negligent-release facts than tests true internal-only deployment. I'm keeping the claim but marking that sub-clause as the genuine soft spot rather than defending it on resolution speed, which was the wrong axis.

Newly dangerous on the other branch: if the federal duty-of-care vehicle with express preemption advances (ai-pressure), it could foreclose the state-level test case pressure-model's pivot depends on, before SB 53 is ever tested against this conduct.
